title: Trump Can’t Rally the Republicans He Needs
excerpt: Trump can’t rally the Republicans he needs. The GOP’s midterms problem isn’t the MAGA base. It’s the Trump 2024 voters who don’t think he’s doing that great a job.
content:
The heart of the 2026 midterm-election battle is a struggle for the high ground of public opinion between supporters and opponents of the president of the United States. That’s generally true of midterm elections, and it’s particularly true given the unparalleled visibility — ubiquity, really — of Donald Trump and the polarizing effect he has on the whole country. The outcome of the 2026 midterms may depend on whether 2024 Trump supporters bother to go to vote at all. The “enthusiasm gap” between self-identified Democrats and Republicans shows up all the time in the polls, as the Washington Post noted last month:

Americans prefer Democrats to Republicans in the congressional midterm elections by only a slim margin, but Democratic supporters are far more motivated to vote, according to a Washington Post-Ipsos poll.


Because of partisan redistricting that favors Republicans this year, analysts estimate that Democrats need to win by three to four percentage points overall to gain a majority in the House. The poll shows Democrats leading Republicans by about that margin, 48 percent to 45 percent.


The blue advantage grows to eight points among those “absolutely certain to vote,” with 53 percent of highly motivated voters supporting Democrats and 45 percent supporting Republicans.

The enthusiasm gap has also been demonstrated by turnout in recent special and primary elections, as Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter points out:

According to data compiled by The Downballot, Democratic candidates in special elections for legislative and congressional seats this cycle have outperformed Vice President Kamala Harris’ share of the 2024 vote by an average of 12.5 points.


Democratic turnout in primaries has also surged. In Texas’ Senate primaries this March, almost 150,000 more Democrats turned out to vote than Republicans. In Washington state, where the August top-two primary results have been predictive of November election results, former Washington state GOP party chair Chris Vance wrote that the results from the Aug. 4 primary portend “a big blue wave, both locally and nationally.”

Much has been said about possible splits in MAGA land and disappointment in that world with Trump’s agenda and his promises to avenge their grievances. But MAGA folk are not his problem. According to the latest major poll, from Economist-YouGov, 91 percent of self-identified MAGA supporters give Trump a thumbs-up for his job performance, with 62 percent strongly approving of it. But presidential job approval drops to 80 percent among Republicans generally and is also at 80 percent among 2024 Trump voters.

Amy Walter strongly supports the idea that the lack of GOP enthusiasm is from non-MAGA Republicans and other previous Trump voters outside his hard-core base:

[T]he enthusiasm gap isn’t about Trump superfans. The kind of voter who shows up to a rally in Myrtle Beach on a steamy August day probably isn’t at risk of staying home in the fall. Almost two-thirds of those who identified as MAGA Republicans in the July Fox News poll said they were “extremely motivated” to vote. But, in the group of Republicans who said they don’t identify as MAGA, that share fell to just 41%.


Why the gap? Unlike the MAGA Republicans, these less Trump-y GOP voters are more pessimistic about the economy (70% rate it fair/poor compared to just 48% of non-MAGA Republicans), and they also tend to disapprove of the job the president is doing on inflation and the economy. In other words, these voters are more sensitive to the environment around them than they are committed to the president.

Trump’s reported impulse is to reinforce Democratic efforts to make the midterms a referendum on his job performance, and to convince his supporters to think of him as being on the ballot. This may be fundamentally misguided. The people who can’t get enough of Donald Trump already view every election and every political event as representing an opportunity to display their love for him. Forcing others to make their midterm votes reflect their opinion of the president could backfire. His overall job-approval ratio, after all, has been far underwater (currently minus-19.6 percent at Silver Bulletin) all year.

What might work to get the problem voters to wake up and vote? One Republican gave Walter a clear answer:

“You cannot solve a motivation problem by talking about the party brand,” one seasoned GOP strategist told me. “Nobody sitting on their couch in October gets off it because of partisanship. What moves depressed base voters is threat. It is anger.”


Republicans are running out of time to identify what that threat — the kind that would motivate otherwise apathetic GOP voters — looks like.


In June of 2022, the Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade served that role to wake up an equally lethargic Democratic base and prevent a catastrophic November loss. This year, however, it’s more likely that Republicans are going to have to work to make individual Democratic candidates seem particularly sinister.

Calling the opposition as “Dumocrats” or “communists” is already getting old. Pretending Democrats are all eager to reopen the borders so that criminal aliens can rape and kill while they draw welfare benefits and illegally vote might appeal to Trump’s MAGA superfans, but it’s unclear how much traction that gets elsewhere. It would probably make the president crazy if past Trump voters are just too “meh” about him to get off the couch. Doing a better job addressing public concerns over the economy would help. But time’s running out for that, and Trump continues to convey the sense that he’s insulted by the perceived need to convince people they’ve never had it so good. It’s downright discouraging.
